regions.name: Navarra
regions.summary: Navarra sits east of Rioja, running from the Pyrenean foothills down to the Ebro, and the exam remembers it for one thing first: dry Garnacha rosado, deep pink, made by bleeding the vat. The denomination is older than most, recognised under the 1933 wine statute, and it holds five subzones that climb from the hot southern Ribera Baja to the cool, damp Valdizarbe near Pamplona. Garnacha was the historic red; Tempranillo has since overtaken it in the plantings, with Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Chardonnay trialled here earlier than almost anywhere in Spain. Three single-estate Vinos de Pago sit inside its borders, and a corner of DOCa Rioja does too.

terroir.climate: Three climates meet in one province. The north and west, Valdizarbe and Tierra Estella, feel the Atlantic: cooler, wetter, with spring frost a worry. The middle is continental, with hot summers and cold winters. The south, Ribera Baja around Tudela, is semi-arid and Mediterranean in temper, the driest ground in the denomination beside the Bardenas Reales badlands. The cierzo, a cold dry wind from the north west, scours the Ebro valley and keeps rot away.
terroir.soils: Clay and limestone dominate the higher ground, often reddish and stony, with marl in the cooler north. The Ebro and its tributaries, the Arga, Ega and Aragón, laid alluvial terraces of gravel and sand in the Riberas. Baja Montaña's soils are shallow and poor, which suits old bush Garnacha.
terroir.topography: The vineyard drops from around 600 metres under the Pyrenean foothills to about 250 metres on the Ebro plain. Baja Montaña is hilly and broken, Valdizarbe and Tierra Estella are valleys threaded by the pilgrim road to Santiago, Ribera Alta is open rolling farmland around Olite, and Ribera Baja is flat river plain.
terroir.water: The Ebro forms the southern spine, and its irrigation channels make Ribera Baja's farming possible. The Arga, Ega and Aragón rivers run down from the mountains to meet it, each carving a subzone's valley. Rainfall falls from more than 700 millimetres in the north to about half that in the south.

grapes.name: Grenache / Garnacha
grapes.styles: The historic grape, once nearly all the vineyard: dry deep-coloured rosado by sangrado, and from old bush vines in Baja Montaña, savoury, peppery reds that have drawn a new generation of growers.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.styles: Now the most planted red, giving Crianza and Reserva reds in the Rioja mould, often blended with Cabernet Sauvignon or Merlot rather than with Garnacha.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Planted from the 1980s after the regional research station's trials; firm, cassis-led reds alone or as the backbone of blends, and a mainstay of the pago estates.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Softens Tempranillo and Cabernet blends and makes plump varietal reds in Ribera Alta.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Barrel-fermented whites of real polish from the cooler north and from the pago estates; Navarra took to the grape before most of Spain.

grapes.name: Graciano
grapes.styles: A perfumed, acid-rich seasoning in Tempranillo blends, as in Rioja next door.

grapes.name: Moscatel de Grano Menudo
grapes.styles: The small-berried Muscat, grown in Ribera Baja for late-harvest sweet whites that are orange-blossom scented and gently honeyed.

grapes.name: Viura
grapes.styles: Rioja's Macabeo under its northern name, for fresh, neutral dry whites.

wines.note: Garnacha bled off the skins after a short maceration, so it is darker and fuller than Provence pink: strawberry, watermelon, a bitter twist, bone dry. Serve well chilled with charcuterie, grilled vegetables or a spiced fish dish.
Tempranillo with Cabernet or Merlot, a year or so in oak: red plum, vanilla, soft tannin. A steady match for roast lamb or a pork chop.

From Baja Montaña bush vines, often unoaked or in neutral wood: raspberry, white pepper, dried herbs, with the lift that high ground gives. Pour it slightly cool with grilled meats or a mushroom dish.
Late-harvest Moscatel de Grano Menudo, unfortified, orange blossom and apricot with clean acidity. A small cold glass with a fruit tart or a blue cheese.

made.viticulture: Navarra was Spain's laboratory. The regional government's viticultural research station, founded in 1981, ran the variety trials that brought Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Chardonnay into a vineyard that had been almost entirely Garnacha, and growers followed the results into trellised, drip-irrigated plantings in the Riberas. The old pattern survives in Baja Montaña, where bush-trained Garnacha of fifty years and more stands on thin hillside soils, picked by hand and prized for rosado and for the new wave of varietal reds. Harvest runs from early September in Ribera Baja to October in the cool north, where frost in late spring and rain at vintage are the hazards; in the south the dangers are heat and drought, and the cierzo wind that dries the canopy also strips water from the vine.
made.winemaking: The rosado is made by sangrado, the Spanish word for saignée: whole Garnacha grapes go into the tank, the juice sits on the skins for some hours, and a portion is bled off to ferment cool on its own, which is why Navarra pink is deeper in colour and fuller in body than a pressed pink. Reds follow the national ageing vocabulary, Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva, and the floors set by Spanish law are the baseline every denomination must meet: a red Crianza two years with six months in cask, a Reserva three years with twelve in cask, a Gran Reserva five years with eighteen in cask. Navarra's own rulebook may ask more of a Crianza's cask time than that floor, but it does not use Rioja's stricter clock, and a Gran Reserva here is not Rioja's twenty-four months of cask. French oak is more common here than in Rioja, and many modern reds are released as Roble or without an ageing term. Chardonnay is often barrel-fermented on its lees, and the sweet Moscatel is made by late harvest, sometimes with a few weeks of drying, and fermented to a natural stop.

law.classification: DO Navarra is one denomination with five subzones named on the label only as a geographic claim, never as a tier: Baja Montaña, Valdizarbe, Tierra Estella, Ribera Alta and Ribera Baja. Above it, and outside it in law, stand three Vinos de Pago, single estates granted their own denomination under the 2003 wine law: Pago de Arínzano in 2007, Prado de Irache in 2008 and Pago de Otazu in 2009. A pago wine is not a DO Navarra wine. The south-western corner of the province, around San Adrián and Andosilla, lies within DOCa Rioja's Oriental zone, so a Navarra address can carry a Rioja label. Ageing terms are the national ones, with the national floors as the baseline.

places.name: Baja Montaña
places.note: The north-eastern hills under the Pyrenees, around Sangüesa, highest and poorest in soil: the stronghold of old bush Garnacha, source of the finest rosado and of the varietal reds that have revived the grape's name.

places.name: Valdizarbe
places.note: The north-centre, the Arga valley near Pamplona and Puente la Reina on the pilgrim road: the coolest and wettest subzone, Atlantic in feel, with Chardonnay and Tempranillo on clay-limestone and Pago de Otazu on its edge.

places.name: Tierra Estella
places.note: The west, along the Ega towards the Rioja Alavesa border and the Urbasa range: mixed soils, Atlantic rain, Tempranillo and Cabernet, and the first two pagos, Arínzano and Prado de Irache.

places.name: Ribera Alta
places.note: The open centre around Olite, Tafalla and Marcilla, the largest subzone by vineyard: continental, with Tempranillo, Cabernet and Merlot on alluvial and clay soils, and Olite's castle and wine museum as its landmark.

places.name: Ribera Baja
places.note: The hot dry south around Tudela on the Ebro plain, beside the Bardenas Reales badlands: Garnacha, Tempranillo and the Moscatel de Grano Menudo for sweet wine, with irrigation from the river.

places.name: Pago de Arínzano
places.note: The first Vino de Pago in northern Spain, recognised in 2007, an estate in Tierra Estella built around Tempranillo, Merlot and Chardonnay on the banks of the Ega.

places.name: Pago de Otazu
places.note: A pago of 2009 near Pamplona, Navarra's most northerly, on an estate with a medieval tower where Cabernet, Merlot and Chardonnay ripen in a cool Atlantic-touched valley.

producers.name: Chivite
producers.why: The reference house of Navarra, with family records reaching back to 1647 and the Colección 125 wines that showed Navarra Chardonnay and rosado could age.

producers.name: Bodegas Ochoa
producers.why: An Olite family house whose rosado and Moscatel are the textbook examples of the denomination's two traditional styles.

producers.name: Domaines Lupier
producers.why: Old bush Garnacha from scattered Baja Montaña parcels, the wine that made the world look again at Navarra's historic grape.

producers.name: Artazu
producers.why: A Rioja Alavesa house's Garnacha project in Valdizarbe, proof that Navarra's cool north can make serious varietal red.

producers.name: Bodegas Nekeas
producers.why: A co-operative of family growers in Valdizarbe whose Chardonnay and Garnacha are the best-value introduction to the north.

producers.name: Pago de Arínzano
producers.why: The estate behind the region's first Vino de Pago, Tempranillo and Chardonnay in a modern cellar on the Ega.

producers.name: Bodegas Otazu
producers.why: The Pago de Otazu estate, Navarra's most northerly pago, for Cabernet-led reds and barrel-fermented Chardonnay.

producers.name: Viña Zorzal
producers.why: Young-vine and old-vine Garnacha and Graciano from the Riberas, pouring by the glass across the world as a fresh face of Navarra.

exam: Name the grape and the method of Navarra rosado: Garnacha, bled by sangrado.
Place Navarra on the map: east of Rioja, Pyrenees to the Ebro, and know that a corner of Rioja Oriental lies inside the province.
List the five subzones from north to south and say which is coolest and which hottest.
Know the three Vinos de Pago in Navarra and that a pago is its own denomination, not a DO Navarra tier.
Know why Cabernet, Merlot and Chardonnay are here: the research station's trials of the 1980s.
Give the national ageing floors and say how Rioja's stricter clock differs from them.
traps: Navarra does not use Rioja's ageing clock: a candidate who gives Rioja's twenty-four months of cask for a Gran Reserva is wrong here, where the national floor of eighteen applies.
Rosado from Navarra is dry and dark; it is not a sweet blush and it is not a pressed Provence pink.
Tempranillo, not Garnacha, is now the most planted grape, though Garnacha is the one the exam associates with the region.
Pago de Arínzano, Prado de Irache and Otazu are Vinos de Pago, outside DO Navarra; they are not Navarra Gran Reservas.
Ribera Alta and Ribera Baja are subzones of Navarra; do not confuse them with Ribera del Duero or with Rioja Oriental, which was once Rioja Baja.

cards.b: Garnacha, made by sangrado (bleeding the vat after a short maceration): dry, deep pink, fuller than a pressed rosé.

cards.f: Navarra's five subzones, north to south
cards.b: Baja Montaña, Valdizarbe, Tierra Estella, Ribera Alta, Ribera Baja. Valdizarbe coolest and wettest; Ribera Baja hottest and driest.

cards.f: The three Vinos de Pago in Navarra
cards.b: Pago de Arínzano (2007), Prado de Irache (2008), Pago de Otazu (2009). Each is its own denomination, not part of DO Navarra.

cards.f: Most planted red grape in Navarra today
cards.b: Tempranillo. Garnacha was the historic grape and still defines rosado and the old-vine reds of Baja Montaña.

cards.f: Why Cabernet, Merlot and Chardonnay grow in Navarra
cards.b: The regional viticultural research station, founded 1981, trialled them; growers planted on its results from the 1980s.

cards.f: National ageing floors for a Spanish red
cards.b: Crianza two years, six months cask. Reserva three years, twelve months cask. Gran Reserva five years, eighteen months cask. Rioja is stricter.

cards.f: Navarra's sweet wine grape
cards.b: Moscatel de Grano Menudo (small-berried Muscat), late harvested in Ribera Baja, unfortified.

cards.f: Which neighbouring DOCa reaches into Navarra?
cards.b: Rioja: its Oriental zone includes towns in south-western Navarra such as San Adrián and Andosilla.

questions.q: Which grape makes the traditional dry rosado of Navarra?
questions.exp: Garnacha, bled off the skins by sangrado, gives Navarra's deep dry pink. Tempranillo has overtaken it in the red plantings, but the rosado tradition belongs to Garnacha.

questions.q: Which of Navarra's five subzones is the hottest and driest?
questions.exp: Ribera Baja lies on the Ebro plain around Tudela, semi-arid beside the Bardenas Reales badlands. Valdizarbe and Tierra Estella feel the Atlantic and are the coolest and wettest; Baja Montaña is high hill country under the Pyrenees.

questions.q: Which category of Spanish wine law covers Arínzano, Prado de Irache and Otazu in Navarra?
questions.exp: Each is a Vino de Pago, a single estate with its own denomination under the 2003 wine law, recognised in 2007, 2008 and 2009; none is a DO Navarra wine. DOCa is the rung of Rioja and Priorat, and Vino de la Tierra is country wine.

questions.q: What is the Spanish name for the bleeding method by which Navarra's rosado is drawn off the skins?
questions.exp: Sangrado is the Spanish name for saignée: juice is bled off red grapes after some hours on the skins and fermented on its own, giving a deeper, fuller pink.

questions.q: Which river flows through the south of Navarra past Tudela?
questions.exp: The Ebro runs along the south of the province, where its channels irrigate Ribera Baja. The Duero drains the northern plateau, the Tajo central Spain and the Guadalquivir Andalucía.

questions.q: Under the national ageing floors that apply in Navarra, how many months must a red Gran Reserva spend in cask?
questions.exp: Spanish law sets a red Gran Reserva at five years in all with at least eighteen months in cask of 330 litres or less. Rioja raises its own floor to twenty-four months in cask and twenty-four in bottle.

questions.q: Which subzone of Navarra holds the old bush-vine Garnacha of the Pyrenean foothills around Sangüesa?
questions.exp: Baja Montaña, the north-eastern hill country, keeps the oldest Garnacha on the poorest soils; its rosado and varietal reds are the region's calling card.

regions.name: Penedès (Cava)
regions.summary: Penedès is the Catalan country south west of Barcelona, climbing from the coast to 800 metres, and it is where Cava was born in 1872 at Sant Sadurní d'Anoia. Hold the two names apart: DO Penedès is a place, making still wines and its own organic sparkling called Clàssic Penedès; DO Cava is a traditional-method sparkling wine defined by method and registered vineyards, most of it from Penedès but with authorised zones in the Ebro valley, Extremadura and Valencia. Cava rests on Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada, needs nine months on its lees, and since 2022 is sold as Cava de Guarda or, from eighteen months, Cava de Guarda Superior. Leading estates under the Corpinnat mark left the DO in 2019.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean, softened by the sea on the coast and cooled by altitude inland. Summers are warm and dry, winters mild, and rain arrives in spring and autumn, around 500 millimetres a year. The high Penedès ripens weeks later than the shore, which is the whole reason the three grapes can be grown for acidity rather than weight.
terroir.soils: Mostly calcareous: limestone and chalky clay with sand and gravel on the lower terraces, deeper clay in the central basin, thinner stonier limestone on the high slopes. The lime holds moisture through the dry summer and gives Xarel·lo its firm, saline edge.
terroir.topography: Three steps. The Baix Penedès or Penedès Marítim runs along the coast at low altitude; the Penedès Central is a broad basin around Vilafranca and Sant Sadurní between 200 and 500 metres; the Alt Penedès or Penedès Superior climbs into the foothills of the Catalan pre-coastal range to about 800 metres under Montserrat's jagged outline to the north.
terroir.water: The Anoia and Foix rivers cut the central basin on their way to the sea, and the Cava zone's main Catalan subzone is named for their valleys. The Mediterranean moderates the coast and sends the sea breeze inland on summer afternoons.

grapes.name: Macabeo
grapes.styles: Rioja's Viura under its Catalan name: the fruit and apple freshness of the Cava blend, early picked, gentle in acidity. Also the base of simple still whites.

grapes.name: Xarel·lo
grapes.styles: The structural grape, giving body, a waxy saline grip and the capacity to age on lees for years; the long-aged Cavas and most Corpinnat wines lean on it, and it makes serious still white too.

grapes.name: Parellada
grapes.styles: The high-altitude grape of the Alt Penedès, late ripening, light and floral, bringing acidity and delicacy to the blend; it fades out of the longest-aged wines.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Permitted in Cava since the 1980s and used for richness in premium white cuvées; also a still varietal in the cooler hills.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Allowed for Cava, white or rosado, lending red fruit and depth to pink cuvées.

grapes.name: Trepat
grapes.styles: A Catalan red from Conca de Barberà, permitted in Cava only for rosado, giving pale, strawberry-scented pink wine.

grapes.name: Grenache / Garnacha
grapes.styles: A permitted red for Cava rosado and a mainstay of still reds in the warm Baix Penedès.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre / Monastrell
grapes.styles: A permitted red for Cava rosado, and the historic coastal red of the Baix Penedès.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The grape of the Penedès still-wine revival of the 1960s and 1970s, making structured reds in the central basin.

wines.note: Apple, citrus, a little bread from nine months or more on the lees, at under twelve grams of sugar. Serve at 6 to 8 °C as an aperitif or with fried food, tapas and salt.
Thirty months or more on the lees and no added sugar: toasted bread, dried apple, honeyed depth with a saline Xarel·lo finish. A wine for the table, with rice dishes, roast chicken or aged cheese.
At least a quarter red grapes, usually Trepat, Garnacha or Pinot Noir: strawberry and redcurrant, dry and brisk. Chill well and pour with charcuterie or grilled prawns.
DO Penedès's own traditional-method sparkling, organic by rule and at least fifteen months on the lees; a Catalan alternative to Cava with the same grapes and often a drier, more vinous frame.
Still, dry and textured: quince, fennel, salt and a bitter-almond finish, sometimes aged in old wood or amphora. Pair with grilled fish, anchovies or a tomato bread with olive oil.

made.viticulture: The Cava vineyard is spread across many small growers who sell to the big houses, and the blend is organised by altitude: Macabeo ripens first on the lower and central land, Xarel·lo in the middle, Parellada last on the high ground, where it can hang into late September and still hold acidity. Vines are mostly trellised today, with old Xarel·lo bush vines kept for the best wines, and yields are capped by the DO. Harvest begins in August for sparkling, earlier than for still wine, because the base must stay below about eleven degrees of alcohol with acidity intact. Drought is the pressing hazard, and the lime-rich soils and mild sea air mitigate it. The 2022 rules push the top of the pyramid towards the land: a Cava de Guarda Superior must come from vines at least ten years old, hand harvested, from a registered plot yielding no more than 10,000 kilograms per hectare, and organic from the 2025 harvest. Corpinnat already demands organic farming and hand picking of every member, and Clàssic Penedès organic farming.
made.winemaking: Cava is made by the traditional method: a still base wine is bottled with sugar and yeast, ferments a second time in that bottle, rests on the dead yeast for at least nine months, and is riddled, disgorged and dosed in the same glass the guest is served from. The minimum pressure is 3.5 atmospheres. Blending is the craft; most houses marry the three Catalan grapes across subzones, and the longest-aged wines favour Xarel·lo because Parellada's delicacy fades. Ageing tiers are set by months on the lees: nine for Cava de Guarda, eighteen for Reserva, thirty for Gran Reserva, thirty-six for Cava de Paraje Calificado, the single-estate top tier created in 2017. A Gran Reserva may only be Brut Nature, Extra Brut or Brut. Dosage terms follow the European scale: Brut Nature under three grams with nothing added, Extra Brut under six, Brut under twelve, Extra Seco twelve to seventeen, Seco seventeen to thirty-two, Semi Seco thirty-two to fifty, Dulce above fifty. Rosado needs at least a quarter of red grapes in the blend, never a blend of finished white and red.

law.classification: Two denominations overlap on the same ground. DO Penedès, regulated in 1960, is a geographic denomination for still wines and for Clàssic Penedès, its organic traditional-method sparkling with fifteen months on the lees. DO Cava is a denomination for traditional-method sparkling wine from registered vineyards in four zones: Comtats de Barcelona in Catalonia, Valle del Ebro in Rioja, Navarra, Álava and Aragón, Viñedos de Almendralejo in Extremadura, and the Zona de Levante around Requena in Valencia. Its rules published in the BOE in June 2021, applied to labels from 1 January 2022, split the wine into Cava de Guarda, nine months on the lees, and Cava de Guarda Superior, which holds Reserva at eighteen months, Gran Reserva at thirty and Cava de Paraje Calificado at thirty-six, and which must be vintage dated and, from the 2025 harvest, organic. Corpinnat is a private collective mark, not a denomination: its members left DO Cava in 2019 and label their wines with the mark in place of a DO.

Cava de Guarda Superior: Gran Reserva

Corpinnat

labels: Under three grams of sugar a litre and no dosage added.
Under twelve grams a litre, the common dry style.
Seventeen to thirty-two and thirty-two to fifty grams, off-dry to sweet, contrary to what the words suggest.
A pink Cava with at least a quarter red grapes in the blend.
The Catalan Cava zone, with subzones such as Valls d'Anoia-Foix and Serra de Mar.

places.name: Sant Sadurní d'Anoia
places.note: The Cava capital in the Penedès Central, where the first bottles were made in 1872 and where the largest houses keep their cellars; most Cava is still made in and around the town.

places.name: Vilafranca del Penedès
places.note: The administrative heart of DO Penedès and the historic wine town of the central basin, seat of the Consejo and home of the big still-wine houses.

places.name: Penedès Superior
places.note: The Alt Penedès, the high inland slopes up to 800 metres below Montserrat: Parellada's home, with Chardonnay, Riesling and other cool-climate whites in the coolest corners.

places.name: Penedès Central
places.note: The broad calcareous basin between 200 and 500 metres around Vilafranca and Sant Sadurní, where Macabeo and Xarel·lo for Cava share the land with still reds and whites.

places.name: Penedès Marítim
places.note: The Baix Penedès along the coast, the warmest step: Monastrell and Garnacha reds, early-ripening Macabeo, and the sea breeze that keeps the coastal vineyards healthy.

places.name: Conca del Riu Anoia
places.note: The name one leading estate took in 2012 when it left Cava to make traditional-method wine under its own stricter charter, a precedent for the Corpinnat exit of 2019.

places.name: Valls d'Anoia-Foix
places.note: A subzone of the Comtats de Barcelona Cava zone, the valleys of the two rivers around Sant Sadurní, the densest Cava country of all.

places.name: Cava outside Catalonia
places.note: Three further zones carry the DO: Valle del Ebro in Rioja, Navarra, Álava and Aragón, Viñedos de Almendralejo in Extremadura, and Zona de Levante around Requena in Valencia, where Macabeo also dominates.

producers.name: Codorníu
producers.why: The house where Cava began in 1872, with Anna de Codorníu the first Chardonnay Cava and a modernist cellar at Sant Sadurní.

producers.name: Freixenet
producers.why: The other giant of Sant Sadurní, whose black-bottled Cordon Negro put Cava into the world's supermarkets.

producers.name: Gramona
producers.why: A founding Corpinnat house known for very long lees ageing on Xarel·lo and a biodynamic estate at Sant Sadurní.

producers.name: Recaredo
producers.why: Corpinnat, biodynamic, every wine Brut Nature and hand disgorged, the reference for terroir-driven Catalan sparkling.

producers.name: Raventós i Blanc
producers.why: The estate that left Cava in 2012 for its own Conca del Riu Anoia designation, from the family that made the first Cava.

producers.name: Juvé y Camps
producers.why: Family house at Sant Sadurní whose Reserva de la Familia Brut Nature is a benchmark for aged traditional Cava.

producers.name: Torres
producers.why: The dominant still-wine house of Vilafranca, whose Mas La Plana Cabernet put Penedès reds on the international map in the 1970s.

producers.name: Jean Leon
producers.why: The 1960s pioneer of varietal Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay in Penedès, in the Torres family's hands since the mid 1990s.

producers.name: Agustí Torelló Mata
producers.why: A Sant Sadurní family house famous for Kripta, a long-aged Gran Reserva in an amphora-shaped bottle.

producers.name: Llopart
producers.why: A grower family that claims sparkling wine on its hill above Sant Sadurní since 1887 and now works under Corpinnat.

Recite the lees ladder: Guarda nine, Reserva eighteen, Gran Reserva thirty, Paraje Calificado thirty-six, and know Gran Reserva is Brut or drier.
Separate DO Penedès, a place with its own Clàssic Penedès sparkling, from DO Cava, a method with four zones across Spain.
Know the four Cava zones and that Comtats de Barcelona holds most of the wine.
Know the dosage scale, especially that Brut Nature is under three grams with nothing added and Seco is off-dry.
Know Corpinnat as the 2019 secession, a collective mark outside the DO, and the date Cava began, 1872 at Sant Sadurní.
Place the three steps of Penedès and which grape ripens on each.
traps: Cava is traditional method, bottle fermented; a candidate who says tank or Charmat is confusing it with Prosecco.
The grapes are the Catalan trio first; Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are permitted but not the base of the style.
Cava's nine-month minimum is the shortest of Champagne, Franciacorta and Cava; the three numbers get swapped.
Penedès is not Cava: a Penedès label can be still wine or Clàssic Penedès, and Cava can come from Rioja, Navarra, Extremadura or Valencia.
Corpinnat is not a tier of Cava and not a DO; it is a private mark of houses that left the DO in 2019.
Seco on a sparkling label means off-dry, seventeen to thirty-two grams, not dry; Brut Nature is the driest term.
The old Rueda and Rioja habit of calling Macabeo Viura can hide the fact that it is the same grape as Cava's Macabeo.

cards.f: The three traditional Cava grapes and what each gives
cards.b: Macabeo: fruit and freshness. Xarel·lo: body, structure and ageing. Parellada: acidity and delicacy from the high Penedès.

cards.f: Cava lees ladder, in months
cards.b: Cava de Guarda 9. Guarda Superior: Reserva 18, Gran Reserva 30, Cava de Paraje Calificado 36. Gran Reserva only Brut Nature, Extra Brut or Brut.

cards.f: Cava's four zones
cards.b: Comtats de Barcelona (Catalonia, most of the wine), Valle del Ebro (Rioja, Navarra, Álava, Aragón), Viñedos de Almendralejo (Extremadura), Zona de Levante (Requena, Valencia).

cards.f: Cava dosage scale, grams per litre
cards.b: Brut Nature under 3, no sugar added. Extra Brut under 6. Brut under 12. Extra Seco 12 to 17. Seco 17 to 32. Semi Seco 32 to 50. Dulce over 50.

cards.f: First Cava: where and when
cards.b: Sant Sadurní d'Anoia, Penedès, 1872, by the Codorníu house after a study of Champagne, using the local white grapes.

cards.f: What is Corpinnat?
cards.b: A private collective mark of leading Penedès sparkling houses that left DO Cava in 2019: estate fruit, organic, hand picked, 18 months minimum on lees.

cards.f: What is Clàssic Penedès?
cards.b: DO Penedès's own traditional-method sparkling: organic by rule, at least 15 months on the lees, never called Cava.

cards.f: Cava rosado rule
cards.b: At least a quarter of the blend must be red grapes (Trepat, Garnacha, Pinot Noir, Monastrell); no blending of finished white and red wine.

cards.f: Three steps of Penedès and their grapes
cards.b: Marítim (coast): Monastrell, Garnacha, early Macabeo. Central (200 to 500 m): Macabeo, Xarel·lo. Superior (to 800 m): Parellada, Chardonnay.

cards.f: Cava de Guarda Superior vineyard rules
cards.b: Vines at least ten years old, hand harvested, registered plot, yield capped at 10,000 kg per hectare, vintage dated, organic from the 2025 harvest.

questions.q: Which Cava grape gives the blend its body and its capacity for long lees ageing?
questions.exp: Xarel·lo is the structural grape; Macabeo brings fruit, Parellada acidity from the high vineyards. Trepat is a red permitted only for rosado.

questions.q: What is the minimum time on the lees for a Cava Gran Reserva?
questions.exp: Gran Reserva needs thirty months. Nine is the floor for Cava de Guarda, eighteen for Reserva and thirty-six for Cava de Paraje Calificado.

questions.q: In which town of the Penedès was the first Cava made in 1872?
questions.exp: Sant Sadurní d'Anoia remains the Cava capital. Vilafranca is DO Penedès's administrative town, Vilanova i la Geltrú the coastal port of the Garraf and El Vendrell the chief town of the Baix Penedès.

questions.q: Which sweetness term on a Cava label means fewer than three grams of sugar per litre with no dosage added?
questions.exp: Brut Nature is the driest term and the only one with nothing added. Extra Brut allows under six grams, Brut under twelve, and Seco is in fact off-dry at seventeen to thirty-two.

questions.q: Which Cava zone covers Catalonia and produces most of the denomination's wine?
questions.exp: Comtats de Barcelona is the Catalan zone, with subzones such as Valls d'Anoia-Foix; the other three are Valle del Ebro, Viñedos de Almendralejo and Zona de Levante.

questions.q: What is the name of the collective mark founded by leading Penedès houses that left DO Cava in 2019?
questions.exp: Corpinnat is a private brand, not a denomination; its members farm organically, pick by hand, vinify on the estate and age at least eighteen months on the lees.

questions.q: What is the minimum share of red grapes in the blend of a Cava Rosado?
questions.exp: A rosado must carry at least a quarter red grapes, usually Trepat, Garnacha or Pinot Noir, and may not be made by blending finished white and red wines.

questions.q: Which Cava grape is grown highest, on the slopes of the Alt Penedès?
questions.exp: Parellada needs the altitude of the Penedès Superior to keep its acidity and is picked last; Macabeo ripens first on the lower land and Xarel·lo in the central basin.

regions.name: Priorat
regions.summary: Priorat is a bowl of steep terraces in the Tarragona hills, inland from the Catalan coast, and its name comes from the Carthusian priory of Scala Dei founded there in the twelfth century. Its rock is llicorella, a black slate shot with quartz, and its grapes are old bush Garnacha and Cariñena, joined since the 1980s by Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Merlot. Yields are tiny, alcohol is high and the wines are dense, stony and long lived. Priorat is one of only two Spanish denominations at the top tier, written in Catalan as DOQ, and it has built a Burgundian ladder of its own: village wine, named site, classified vineyard and great classified vineyard.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean with a continental edge: summer days above 35 °C, cool nights because of the altitude and the surrounding ranges, dry winters that can freeze, and rainfall around 400 to 600 millimetres, most of it in autumn and spring storms. The sea is close enough to send humid morning air up the valleys; the Montsant range to the north blocks the colder winds.
terroir.soils: Llicorella: Carboniferous slate and schist, dark brown to black, flaking in thin plates, laced with veins of quartz and almost without organic matter. It drains instantly, reflects heat onto the fruit and forces roots deep into the fractured rock for water. Pockets of clay and granite occur, but slate is the signature the exam wants.
terroir.topography: An amphitheatre of hills between roughly 100 and 750 metres, the vineyards on slopes so steep they are cut into terraces or planted straight up the hillside on costers, the old unterraced pitches. Villages sit at different heights: Gratallops and Bellmunt lower and warmer, Porrera, La Morera de Montsant and Scala Dei higher and cooler, and that difference drives the village wines.
terroir.water: The Siurana river and its tributaries drain the bowl towards the Ebro, and the Siurana reservoir lies to the north east. Water in the vineyard is scarce; vines live on what the slate stores and what their deep roots find.

grapes.name: Grenache / Garnacha
grapes.styles: Garnatxa in Catalan: old bush vines on slate give red fruit turned to liquorice and stone, high alcohol with freshness, the perfume of the region's finest village and site wines.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.styles: Carinyena or Samsó here, Mazuelo in Rioja: on century-old bush vines it gives acidity, black fruit, iron and grip, and the greatest old-vine Priorats of Porrera lean on it.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Brought by the 1980s pioneers for structure and cassis in the modern blends; less planted by the younger generation.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Adds violet and black pepper to the international-styled blends and ripens fully on the lower terraces.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: A softening partner in some modern blends, in retreat as the region returns to its native grapes.

grapes.name: Garnacha Blanca
grapes.styles: The lead white, with Macabeu and Pedro Ximénez, for rich, stony, textured dry whites that are a small but growing part of the denomination.

wines.note: Garnacha and Cariñena, often with Cabernet or Syrah: black cherry, liquorice, graphite and warm stone, high alcohol carried by acidity and firm tannin. Decant young vintages and pour with lamb, game or a rich stew.
A red from one of the twelve named villages, carrying the village on the label; Porrera gives taut Cariñena-led wines, Gratallops riper Garnacha.
Garnacha Blanca, Macabeu and Pedro Ximénez from the slate, sometimes skin-contacted or barrel-aged: pear, fennel, salt and a stony weight. Good with grilled fish and roasted vegetables.
The old fortified and oxidative Garnacha wines of the monks' era, now a tiny production, with a nutty, raisined depth that suits almond pastries and hard cheese.

made.viticulture: Everything here is hand work. Old Garnacha and Cariñena bush vines, many a century old, stand on costers, slopes too steep for terraces, and on narrow terraces where a single row fits; yields from these old vines are among the lowest in Spain because the slate holds almost no water and the vines carry a handful of bunches. Newer plantings since the 1980s are on wider terraces cut by machine, trellised, and include the French grapes the pioneers brought. The hazards are drought, summer heat that can halt ripening, and erosion on the pitches when the autumn storms arrive. Harvest runs from September into October, with Cariñena the last to come in, picked at full ripeness to tame its acidity and tannin. Altitude matters: a village at 600 metres can pick two or three weeks after one at 150, which is why the classification ranks villages and sites rather than only the denomination.
made.winemaking: The modern style was set in the late 1980s at Gratallops by a group of newcomers who made five wines in one shared cellar and sold them as clos, Burgundian in name and Bordeaux-like in make: destemmed fruit, long macerations, new French barriques. Thirty years on the pendulum has swung back towards the native grapes, larger and older oak, some whole bunches and foudres, and lower alcohol where the site allows. Fermentations are mostly in stainless steel or open vats, ageing in French oak of 225 to 500 litres and increasingly in large casks or concrete. Garnacha and Cariñena are often fermented apart and blended before bottling, and the top village and site wines are frequently single varietal Cariñena or Garnacha. Spanish ageing terms exist in the rulebook but the leading houses rarely print them; the vineyard name does the work. Whites are pressed gently, often barrel-fermented on lees, and a few houses still make rancio and sweet Garnacha in the old way.

law.classification: Priorat became a DO in 1954 and was raised to Denominació d'Origen Qualificada by Catalonia in 2000, a status confirmed in national law in 2009; it shares the top rung with Rioja alone. On top of that it layered its own pyramid, village wine first in the late 2000s and the whole ladder presented in May 2019: DOQ Priorat for the denomination, Vi de Vila for a wine from one of twelve named villages, Vi de Paratge for a wine from a named site within a village, Vinya Classificada for a single classified vineyard and Gran Vinya Classificada for the few great ones, of which L'Ermita above Gratallops was the first. Each step up asks for more of the land: lower yields, older vines and a record of bottling the site apart. Montsant, the horseshoe DO around Priorat, was separated from DO Tarragona in 2001 and is not part of the DOQ.
tiers: DOQ Priorat
The denomination at Spain's top tier since 2000 in Catalan law and 2009 nationally, with Rioja the only other.
Vi de Vila
A village wine from one of twelve named villages, in use since the late 2000s.
Vi de Paratge
A wine from a named site, a paratge, within a village, the next step up from 2019.
Vinya Classificada
A single classified vineyard with a track record of bottling on its own.
Gran Vinya Classificada
The highest rung, a great classified vineyard; L'Ermita was the first named, from the 2017 vintage.
labels: Village wine, with the village name on the label.
Old vines, a term the DOQ regulates by vine age.
Steep unterraced slopes planted straight up the hillside.
The slate and quartz soil, often printed on labels as a badge.
Catalan spellings of Garnacha and Cariñena; Samsó is the local name for Cariñena.

places.name: Gratallops
places.note: The village where the 1980s revival began and the clos wines were first made, lower and warmer in the centre of the bowl, with Garnacha-led wines of ripeness and perfume; L'Ermita lies on a steep slope above it.

places.name: Porrera
places.note: High on the eastern side, cooler and later, famous for century-old Cariñena on slate that gives the region's most structured and long-lived village wines.

places.name: Scala Dei
places.note: The hamlet of the ruined Carthusian priory that named the region, at the foot of the Montsant cliffs; high, cool and home to the denomination's oldest working cellar.

places.name: La Morera de Montsant
places.note: The highest village, under the Montsant range, with vineyards above 600 metres giving fresher Garnacha; Scala Dei lies within its municipal bounds but is named apart in the village list.

places.name: Torroja del Priorat
places.note: A central village on the Siurana with a mix of old bush vines and newer terraces, often cited for balance between Gratallops' ripeness and Porrera's tension.

places.name: Poboleda
places.note: North-east, higher and cooler, with Cariñena and Garnacha on steep costers above the Siurana headwaters.

places.name: Bellmunt del Priorat
places.note: The southern village near the old lead mines, lower and warm, with powerful Garnacha-based reds.

places.name: El Lloar, La Vilella Alta and La Vilella Baixa
places.note: Three small western villages above the Montsant river; the two Vilellas sit one above the other on a steep valley side, and all three carry Vi de Vila names.

places.name: Masos de Falset and Solanes del Molar
places.note: The Priorat portions of Falset and El Molar, whose municipalities straddle the DOQ boundary, each given its own village name so that the list reaches twelve.

places.name: Montsant
places.note: The DO that curves round Priorat like a horseshoe, created in 2001 from Tarragona's Falset subzone: the same grapes on more mixed soils, with slate only in places, sold as the affordable neighbour.

producers.name: Álvaro Palacios
producers.why: The Gratallops house behind L'Ermita, the first Gran Vinya Classificada, and Finca Dofí, which carried Priorat into the world's top tier.

producers.name: Clos Mogador
producers.why: The founding estate of the 1989 Gratallops group, whose Garnacha and Cariñena blend remains the reference modern Priorat.

producers.name: Clos Erasmus
producers.why: A tiny Gratallops estate from the same pioneering circle, Garnacha-led and among the most sought-after wines in Spain.

producers.name: Mas Martinet
producers.why: Another of the five original clos, now a leader of the return to native grapes, whole bunches and amphora.

producers.name: Costers del Siurana
producers.why: Maker of Clos de l'Obac, the fifth of the founding clos wines, and a keeper of the region's history.

producers.name: Cellers de Scala Dei
producers.why: The oldest cellar of the modern denomination, bottling since the 1970s beside the ruined priory that gave Priorat its name.

producers.name: Vall Llach
producers.why: A Porrera house built on old Cariñena, whose Mas de la Rosa was among the first Vinya Classificada sites.

producers.name: Mas Doix
producers.why: Poboleda growers with century-old Cariñena and Garnacha, a name for pure village wines of the high north.

producers.name: Terroir al Límit
producers.why: A Torroja house that took Priorat towards whole-bunch, lower-alcohol, Burgundian single-site wines.

exam: Name the soil, llicorella, and describe it: black slate with quartz, free draining, almost no organic matter.
Name the two historic grapes, Garnacha and Cariñena, and the French grapes the 1980s brought.
Know the DOQ status, shared with Rioja alone, and its dates: 2000 in Catalonia, 2009 nationally, DO since 1954.
Recite the ladder: DOQ Priorat, Vi de Vila, Vi de Paratge, Vinya Classificada, Gran Vinya Classificada, and that L'Ermita was the first at the top.
Place Gratallops as the revival village and Porrera as the old Cariñena village, and know Scala Dei as the priory that named the region.
Know Montsant as the horseshoe neighbour, a separate DO since 2001.
Describe the wine: dense, high alcohol, mineral, long lived, and how it is served, decanted, with red meat and game.
traps: Priorat is a DOQ, the Catalan spelling of DOCa; Montsant, Penedès and Tarragona are DOs, and Priorat and Rioja alone hold the top rung.
The slate is llicorella: the Douro's schist and the Mosel's slate are cousins, but the exam wants the local word, so name the rock.
Cariñena is the grape (Carignan, Mazuelo, Samsó), and it is also a DO in Aragón; in Priorat the word means the grape.
Vi de Vila is a village tier below Vi de Paratge; the ladder climbs village, site, vineyard, great vineyard, not the other way.
Garnacha, not Tempranillo, is the lead red; Tempranillo is a minor player in Catalonia under the name Ull de Llebre.
Scala Dei is a place and a cellar, not a grape or a wine style; the priory gave the whole region its name.

cards.f: Priorat's soil: name and description
cards.b: Llicorella: dark Carboniferous slate and schist with quartz veins, free draining, almost no organic matter; roots dig deep for water.

cards.f: Priorat's two historic grapes
cards.b: Garnacha (Garnatxa) and Cariñena (Carinyena, Samsó, Mazuelo). Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Merlot arrived with the 1980s revival.

cards.f: Priorat's appellation status and dates
cards.b: DO 1954. DOQ (Catalan for DOCa) in Catalan law 2000, national confirmation 2009. Shares the top rung with Rioja only.

cards.f: Priorat's vineyard ladder, bottom to top
cards.b: DOQ Priorat, Vi de Vila (12 villages, since the late 2000s), Vi de Paratge (named site), Vinya Classificada, Gran Vinya Classificada (full ladder 2019; L'Ermita first).

cards.f: Where the Priorat revival began, and when
cards.b: Gratallops, late 1980s: a group of newcomers made five clos wines in one cellar from the 1989 vintage, with new French oak and Cabernet in the blend.

cards.f: Which DO surrounds Priorat like a horseshoe?
cards.b: Montsant, a DO since 2001, carved from Tarragona's Falset subzone; same grapes, more mixed soils, lower prices.

cards.f: What does Priorat mean, and why?
cards.b: Priory: the Carthusian monastery of Scala Dei, founded in the twelfth century, planted the vines and ruled the villages.

cards.f: Porrera versus Gratallops
cards.b: Porrera: high, cool, east side, century-old Cariñena, structured and long lived. Gratallops: lower, warmer, centre, Garnacha perfume, the revival village.

questions.q: What is the name of the slate and quartz soil that defines Priorat?
questions.exp: Llicorella is the local word for the dark, flaking Carboniferous slate shot with quartz; it drains instantly and forces roots deep, which is why yields are so low.

questions.q: Which two grapes make up the old bush vines of Priorat?
questions.exp: Garnacha and Cariñena were already on the terraces when the newcomers arrived; Cabernet, Syrah and Merlot were planted later. The other pairs belong to Rioja, the Levante and the north west.

questions.q: Which tier of Spanish wine law does Priorat hold?
questions.exp: Priorat is a Denominación de Origen Calificada, written DOQ in Catalan, a rung it shares with Rioja alone: Catalonia raised it from DO in 2000 and national law confirmed it in 2009. Montsant and Penedès are plain DOs.

questions.q: Which village of Priorat is known for its high, cool slopes and century-old Cariñena vines?
questions.exp: Porrera sits high on the eastern side and its old Cariñena gives the most structured village wines. Gratallops and Bellmunt are lower and warmer, El Lloar a small western village.

questions.q: Which tier stands at the top of Priorat's own vineyard classification?
questions.exp: The ladder climbs from Vi de Vila through Vi de Paratge and Vinya Classificada to Gran Vinya Classificada, the great classified vineyard; L'Ermita was the first so named.

questions.q: Which DO surrounds Priorat on three sides like a horseshoe?
questions.exp: Montsant was carved from DO Tarragona's Falset subzone in 2001 and shares Priorat's grapes on more mixed soils. Conca de Barberà, Terra Alta and Costers del Segre are other Catalan DOs further north or west.

questions.q: What is the name of the Cariñena grape in Rioja, where it plays a minor blending role?
questions.exp: Mazuelo in Rioja, Samsó or Carinyena in Catalonia and Carignan in France are one grape; in Priorat it gives acidity and iron to the old-vine blends.

regions.name: La Mancha
regions.summary: La Mancha is the high dry plateau south of Madrid, Don Quixote's country, and the largest single denomination in Spain, spread across the provinces of Albacete, Ciudad Real, Cuenca and Toledo. It is the engine room of Spanish volume: Airén, the white grape that was long the most planted vine on earth, feeds the brandy stills and the bulk trade, while Tempranillo under its local name Cencibel makes the reds. Bush vines at low density on clay and limestone endure scorching summers and freezing winters with little rain. Around and inside it sit Valdepeñas, the separate DO to the south, and the largest cluster of Spain's single-estate Vinos de Pago.

terroir.climate: Extreme continental: winters that fall below minus ten, summers above forty, and 300 to 400 millimetres of rain a year, most of it in spring and autumn. Sunshine is near constant and humidity low, so fungal disease is rare, but drought and heat are the daily facts and frost in late spring can take a crop.
terroir.soils: Reddish-brown clay and sandy clay over a bed of limestone, often with a hard lime crust close to the surface that roots must break through. The lime holds some winter moisture; the clay is poor and the soils are low in organic matter.
terroir.topography: A broad level plateau at 600 to 700 metres with hardly a hill across its width, broken only by the low Montes de Toledo to the west and the Sierra Morena rising beyond Valdepeñas to the south. The flatness is the point: vineyard, cereal and olive stretch to the horizon.
terroir.water: The Guadiana gathers on the plain at the Tablas de Daimiel wetlands and drains it westward; the Júcar flows east through Cuenca and gives its name to the neighbouring Ribera del Júcar. Irrigation from deep wells, legal since 1996, has reshaped the modern vineyard.

grapes.name: Airén
grapes.styles: The drought-proof white that carpets the plateau: neutral, low in acid and aroma, made into simple dry whites and distilled in quantity for Brandy de Jerez. Modern cool fermentation gives clean, inexpensive wine.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.styles: Cencibel here: ripe, soft, plum-fruited reds, young or in American oak as Crianza and Reserva at prices no other region can match, and the backbone of Valdepeñas.

grapes.name: Grenache / Garnacha
grapes.styles: Historic on the plain and the lead grape of Méntrida to the north west, for warm, soft reds and rosados.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Planted widely since the 1990s for varietal and blended reds under the regional Vino de la Tierra label and in the pago estates.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Suits the heat and gives dark, peppery reds, a mainstay of the pagos and the modern bodegas.

grapes.name: Macabeo
grapes.styles: Fresher than Airén, planted for better dry whites and for blending with Airén.

grapes.name: Verdejo
grapes.styles: Borrowed from Rueda for aromatic, grassy whites that have replaced some Airén in the better vineyards.

grapes.name: Bobal
grapes.styles: The grape of neighbouring Manchuela and Utiel-Requena, dark and acid-rich, at the eastern edge of the plain.

wines.note: Young Cencibel, unoaked or briefly oaked: ripe plum, soft tannin, easy and inexpensive. The glass-pour red of a thousand tapas bars, happy with cured meats and stews.

Cencibel aged in American oak to the national floors, vanilla and dried cherry over a mellow frame; Valdepeñas makes the same style with longer ageing at bargain prices. Serve with roast pork or Manchego cheese.
Airén or Macabeo fermented cool: light, neutral, clean, served very cold with fried fish or as a simple aperitif.

Estate blends of Cabernet, Syrah, Merlot, Petit Verdot and Tempranillo from the single-estate denominations of Castilla-La Mancha, polished, oak-aged and international in style; a match for roast lamb.

made.viticulture: The plateau was planted the way poverty and drought dictated: bush vines spaced wide apart in a square grid, around 1,600 vines to the hectare, so that each could draw on enough soil water to survive a summer with no rain. Airén thrives on this because it tolerates drought and crops reliably, and that is why it covered so much of Spain's vineyard for most of the twentieth century. Since irrigation became legal in 1996 the picture has changed: trellised rows of Tempranillo, Cabernet, Syrah and Macabeo under drip lines, machine harvested at night to keep the fruit cool, often at yields the old vines could never reach. Grubbing-up subsidies from the European Union removed a great deal of Airén, and Tempranillo has drawn level with it as Spain's most planted grape partly because of La Mancha's replanting. Hazards are winter cold, spring frost, hail and above all heat; disease pressure is low in the dry air, which has helped the region become a large source of organic grapes.
made.winemaking: Scale sets the method. Enormous co-operatives and private bodegas ferment in stainless steel at controlled temperature, a revolution that turned flat oxidised Airén into clean neutral white in the 1980s and 1990s. Much of the white crop is still distilled into the base spirit for Brandy de Jerez and other brandies, and some goes to grape must concentrate. Reds are fermented warm and short for young wine or longer for Crianza, which follows the national floors of two years with six months in cask; American oak is traditional and French oak common in the pagos. Valdepeñas kept the old habit of ageing Cencibel for Reserva and Gran Reserva and selling it cheaply, and once made clarete, a pale red of Airén and Cencibel fermented together. The pago estates work like Bordeaux châteaux, with barrel ageing and estate bottling under their own denominations.

law.classification: DO La Mancha, recognised in 1932 under the wine statute and under its own reglamento since the 1970s, covers parts of four provinces and is administered from Alcázar de San Juan. It uses the national ageing terms at their legal floors. Valdepeñas is a separate DO, an enclave in the south of Ciudad Real with its own rules since 1968. Around both lie further DOs of Castilla-La Mancha: Manchuela, Méntrida, Mondéjar, Ribera del Júcar, Uclés and Almansa. The regional country-wine label Vino de la Tierra de Castilla carries much of the modern varietal production. The 2003 wine law created the Vino de Pago, a single estate with its own denomination, and Castilla-La Mancha holds the largest group of them, beginning with Dominio de Valdepusa in Toledo and Finca Élez in Albacete in 2003, followed by Dehesa del Carrizal, Pago Guijoso, Campo de la Guardia and others.
tiers: Vino de Pago
A single estate with its own denomination under the 2003 law; Castilla-La Mancha holds the largest group, Dominio de Valdepusa the first in 2003.
DO La Mancha
The denomination of the plateau, the largest in Spain by area, across Albacete, Ciudad Real, Cuenca and Toledo.
DO Valdepeñas
A separate enclave DO in the south of Ciudad Real, Cencibel and Airén, famous for cheap aged reds.
Vino de la Tierra de Castilla
The regional country-wine label covering the whole autonomous community, home of most varietal and international-style wines.
Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva
National floors: reds two years with six months in cask, three with twelve, five with eighteen.
labels: A young wine with no required ageing.
A pale red once typical of Valdepeñas, red and white grapes fermented together.
An estate; on a label, Vino de Pago means an estate with its own denomination.

places.name: Alcázar de San Juan and the central plain
places.note: The seat of the Consejo and the heart of the DO in Ciudad Real, surrounded by the great co-operative towns such as Tomelloso, Socuéllamos and Campo de Criptana with their windmills.

places.name: Valdepeñas
places.note: A separate DO at the southern edge of the plain before the Sierra Morena, Cencibel and Airén on red clay and lime, known for oak-aged Reserva and Gran Reserva reds sold at everyday prices and for its historic clarete.

places.name: Dominio de Valdepusa
places.note: An estate at Malpica de Tajo in Toledo, the first Vino de Pago in Spain in 2003, planted to Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Petit Verdot and Graciano with drip irrigation on a limestone plateau.

places.name: Finca Élez
places.note: A high estate near Albacete granted pago status in 2003 alongside Valdepusa, Chardonnay, Merlot and Syrah at around 1,000 metres.

places.name: Manchuela
places.note: The DO on the eastern edge towards Valencia, straddling Cuenca and Albacete, where Bobal gives dark, acid-fresh reds and rosados from old bush vines on limestone.

places.name: Méntrida
places.note: A Garnacha DO in Toledo north west of the plain, closer to Madrid, with old bush Garnacha on granite sand in the Gredos foothills drawing new growers.

places.name: Ribera del Júcar and Uclés
places.note: Two young DOs of Cuenca, recognised in the 2000s, Tempranillo and Bobal along the Júcar river and Tempranillo on the Uclés uplands.

producers.name: Dominio de Valdepusa
producers.why: Spain's first Vino de Pago, a Toledo estate whose Cabernet and Syrah showed in the 1990s what the plateau could do with irrigation and canopy science.

producers.name: Finca Élez
producers.why: One of the two pagos recognised in 2003, high in Albacete, for Chardonnay and Merlot of unexpected freshness.

producers.name: Dehesa del Carrizal
producers.why: A Ciudad Real pago in the Montes de Toledo making Cabernet, Syrah and Chardonnay on a hunting estate.

producers.name: Félix Solís
producers.why: The Valdepeñas giant behind Viña Albali, the cheap aged Cencibel that taught the world the words Reserva and Gran Reserva.

producers.name: Bodegas Ayuso
producers.why: A Villarrobledo house whose Estola Reserva was for decades the best-known aged red of DO La Mancha.

producers.name: Vinícola de Castilla
producers.why: A large modern bodega at Manzanares that led the plateau's move into varietal wines under the Castilla label.

producers.name: Finca Antigua
producers.why: A Cuenca estate from a Rioja family, varietal Syrah, Garnacha and Petit Verdot that made La Mancha fashionable by the glass.

producers.name: Bodegas Verum
producers.why: A Tomelloso estate reviving old bush Airén for serious, textured white and making Cencibel with care.

producers.name: Virgen de las Viñas
producers.why: The Tomelloso co-operative, one of the largest wineries in Europe, the face of La Mancha's volume.

exam: Know Airén: Spain's most planted white, drought-proof bush vines, neutral wine and brandy base.
Know Cencibel as Tempranillo's name here, and Tinto Fino, Tinta de Toro and Ull de Llebre as the others.
Place La Mancha: the high plateau south of Madrid across four provinces, the largest DO in Spain.
Separate Valdepeñas, a DO of its own in the south, from DO La Mancha.
Know the Vino de Pago: single estate with its own denomination since 2003, Dominio de Valdepusa first, most of them in Castilla-La Mancha.
Know why irrigation matters: legal since 1996, it rebuilt the vineyard around Tempranillo and the international grapes.
Give the climate in one line: extreme continental, 600 to 700 metres, 300 to 400 millimetres of rain.
traps: Cencibel is Tempranillo, not a separate grape and not Garnacha; the exam loves the synonym list.
Valdepeñas is not a subzone of La Mancha; it is a separate DO, an enclave to the south.
A Vino de Pago is an estate with its own denomination, above DO in prestige; it is not a vineyard term inside DO La Mancha and it is not the same as the private Grandes Pagos de España club.
Airén is a white grape; a candidate who files it with the reds has lost the question.
Tempranillo now rivals Airén for Spain's most planted grape; Airén still leads the whites, but it no longer stands alone at the top of the country.
Vino de la Tierra de Castilla is Castilla-La Mancha's country wine; Vino de la Tierra de Castilla y León is a different region to the north.

cards.f: Tempranillo's name in La Mancha
cards.b: Cencibel. Elsewhere: Tinto Fino and Tinta del País (Ribera del Duero), Tinta de Toro (Toro), Ull de Llebre (Catalonia), Tinta Roriz and Aragonez (Portugal).

cards.f: Airén: what it is and why it matters
cards.b: A drought-tolerant white bush vine, long the most planted grape on earth; neutral dry whites and the base spirit for Brandy de Jerez.

cards.f: La Mancha's four provinces
cards.b: Albacete, Ciudad Real, Cuenca and Toledo, administered from Alcázar de San Juan; the largest DO in Spain by area.

cards.f: Valdepeñas: where and what
cards.b: A separate DO, an enclave in the south of Ciudad Real: Cencibel and Airén, oak-aged Reserva and Gran Reserva reds at low prices.

cards.f: Spain's first Vino de Pago
cards.b: Dominio de Valdepusa, Malpica de Tajo, Toledo, 2003, with Finca Élez the same year; the category came from the 2003 wine law.

cards.f: La Mancha's climate in one line
cards.b: Extreme continental at 600 to 700 metres: winters below minus ten, summers above forty, 300 to 400 mm of rain, constant sun.

cards.f: Why La Mancha's old vineyards are planted so widely
cards.b: Bush vines at about 1,600 per hectare in a square grid, so each vine draws on enough soil water to survive the rainless summer.

cards.f: The country-wine label of Castilla-La Mancha
cards.b: Vino de la Tierra de Castilla, covering the whole autonomous community; not Castilla y León's.

questions.q: What is the local name for Tempranillo in La Mancha and Valdepeñas?
questions.exp: Cencibel is the plateau's name for Tempranillo; the same grape is Tinto Fino in Ribera del Duero and Tinta de Toro in Toro.

questions.q: Which white grape covers most of the La Mancha vineyard?
questions.exp: Airén's drought tolerance made it the most planted vine in the world for decades, and much of its crop is distilled for Brandy de Jerez. Macabeo and Verdejo are newer plantings here; Palomino is Jerez's grape.

questions.q: Which DO is a separate enclave at the southern edge of the La Mancha plain?
questions.exp: Valdepeñas has had its own DO since 1968 and is known for inexpensive oak-aged Cencibel. Manchuela lies to the east with Bobal, Méntrida to the north west with Garnacha, Uclés in Cuenca.

questions.q: In which year was Dominio de Valdepusa recognised as Spain's first Vino de Pago?
questions.exp: The Vino de Pago category was created by the 2003 wine law and Valdepusa, with Finca Élez, was recognised that year. 1991 is Rioja's DOCa, 1996 the legalisation of irrigation, 2009 Priorat's DOQ.

questions.q: In which year did Spain make vineyard irrigation legal, reshaping the plantings of La Mancha?
questions.exp: Irrigation had been forbidden for quality vineyards until 1996; its legalisation let the plateau plant trellised Tempranillo, Cabernet and Syrah under drip lines.

questions.q: Which red grape of neighbouring Manchuela gives dark, acid-fresh wines on the eastern edge of the plateau?
questions.exp: Bobal is Manchuela's and Utiel-Requena's grape. Monastrell belongs to Jumilla and Yecla, Mencía to Bierzo, Garnacha Tintorera to Almansa.

questions.q: What is the country-wine designation that covers the whole of Castilla-La Mancha and carries most of its varietal wines?
accept: Vino de la Tierra de Castilla
vino de la tierra de castilla
questions.ans: Vino de la Tierra de Castilla
questions.exp: Vino de la Tierra de Castilla is the regional IGP for Castilla-La Mancha; Castilla y León to the north has its own, differently named label.

regions.name: Jumilla / Yecla
regions.summary: Jumilla and Yecla are two neighbouring denominations in the dry hill country of Murcia, inland from the Mediterranean, and they share one grape: Monastrell, the vine France calls Mourvèdre, which needs this kind of heat to ripen at all. Jumilla, a DO since 1966, spills from Murcia into six municipalities of Albacete; Yecla, a DO since 1975, is one municipality alone. Both grow old ungrafted bush vines on poor limestone and sand, because phylloxera did not reach Jumilla until 1989. The wines are dark, warm, tannic and generous, from juicy young reds through oaked blends with Syrah and Cabernet to the sweet Dulce Monastrell.

terroir.climate: Continental with Mediterranean summers: more than 3,000 hours of sun, summer afternoons above 40 °C, winter frosts, and around 300 millimetres of rain, falling mostly in violent autumn storms. Altitude between 400 and 800 metres gives cold nights that keep some freshness in a very ripe grape; hail and drought are the main hazards.
terroir.soils: Poor, pale, lime-rich soils: limestone and chalky marl with sandy, stony patches, low in organic matter and free draining. The sand kept phylloxera at bay for a century, which is why ungrafted Monastrell survives here, and the lime holds enough winter water to carry a bush vine through summer.
terroir.topography: High inland plateaux and broad valleys between dry sierras, the vineyards on gentle slopes and plains. Yecla splits into Campo Arriba, the higher northern land up towards 800 metres where the best Monastrell grows, and Campo Abajo, lower and warmer to the south. Jumilla's Albacete portion is higher and cooler than the Murcian heart.
terroir.water: There is no river of consequence; the vineyard lives on winter rain stored in the limestone and, in newer plantings, on drip irrigation from wells. The Mediterranean lies an hour away and sends little relief inland.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre / Monastrell
grapes.styles: The grape of both DOs, late ripening, thick skinned and sun loving: blackberry, dried fig, earth and game, high tannin and alcohol, from juicy unoaked reds to dense oak-aged wines and the sweet Dulce Monastrell.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The modern partner, adding colour, violet and pepper to Monastrell blends and ripening well in the heat.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Structure and cassis in the premium blends that made Jumilla's reputation abroad in the 2000s.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.styles: Cencibel here as on the plateau, planted for softer reds and for blends with Monastrell.

grapes.name: Garnacha Tintorera
grapes.styles: Alicante Bouschet, a red-fleshed grape for colour, more at home in neighbouring Almansa.

grapes.name: Petit Verdot
grapes.styles: A late ripener that enjoys the heat, used for spice and colour in the modern blends.

grapes.name: Airén
grapes.styles: The plateau white, with Macabeo, for simple dry whites that are a small share of both denominations.

grapes.name: Moscatel
grapes.styles: Moscatel de Alejandría for sweet whites and for Jumilla's small output of fortified and late-harvest wine.

wines.note: Unoaked or briefly oaked Monastrell from bush vines: ripe blackberry, fig, a dusty earthy edge, generous alcohol with soft chewy tannin. Serve a touch cool with grilled lamb, sausages or a tomato-rich stew.
Monastrell with Syrah or Cabernet aged in French and American oak: black fruit, cocoa, leather, dense and warm. A wine for braised meats, game and hard cheese.
From the higher northern land of Yecla, the freshest expression of the grape, with more lift and firmer tannin than the valley wines; pair with roast kid or lamb.
Late-harvest Monastrell fermented sweet, sometimes fortified: black fig, chocolate and dried cherry with grippy tannin. A small glass with dark chocolate or a blue cheese.

made.viticulture: Monastrell is a grape of extremes. It buds late and ripens last of all, needs long heat to soften its tannin, and shuts down in drought, so it is grown as a low bush vine, pruned short, spaced wide and left to find water in the limestone. Many vineyards are ungrafted, on their own roots: the sandy soils kept the louse away until 1989, when phylloxera finally reached Jumilla and forced a wave of replanting on rootstock, which also brought Syrah, Cabernet and Petit Verdot into the region and newer trellised, drip-irrigated rows alongside the old bush vines. Yields from old vines are tiny, often under 2,000 kilograms a hectare. Harvest is late, from mid September into October, and timing is everything: too early and the tannin is green, too late and the wine is jammy and the grape prone to shrivel. Hail in summer and the autumn downpour at harvest are the hazards; disease is scarce in the dry air and organic farming is widespread.
made.winemaking: Monastrell reduces easily in the cellar, so it is pumped over and aerated during fermentation and racked early. Young wines are made by short macerations and bottled unoaked to keep the fruit. Premium reds take long macerations and twelve months or more in French or American oak, often blended with Syrah or Cabernet for colour and polish, and the Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva terms follow the national floors. Dulce Monastrell is made from very ripe or partly raisined grapes, fermentation stopped by cold or by spirit to leave sweetness; Jumilla also keeps a tradition of fortified and sweet Moscatel. Historically the region sold doble pasta, a black wine fermented on a double load of skins, as blending material for bulk reds, and that trade is where the modern bodegas learned to handle the grape's colour and tannin.

law.classification: Two separate DOs. Jumilla, regulated in 1966, is unusual in crossing a regional border: its heart is the municipality of Jumilla in Murcia, but six municipalities of Albacete in Castilla-La Mancha, around Hellín, Tobarra, Ontur, Fuente Álamo, Albatana and Montealegre del Castillo, are inside it. Yecla, a DO since 1975, is the only Spanish denomination made of a single municipality, and it names two subzones, Campo Arriba and Campo Abajo. Both use the national ageing terms. A varietal label follows the national rule of at least 85 per cent of the named grape. Around them lie Bullas, a Murcian DO of 1994 further south, Alicante to the east with its Fondillón, and Almansa to the north in Albacete with Garnacha Tintorera.

A DO since 1975 from the single municipality of Yecla in Murcia, with subzones Campo Arriba and Campo Abajo.
Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva
The national floors: reds two years with six months in cask, three with twelve, five with eighteen.
Dulce Monastrell
Jumilla's sweet red, late-harvest or fortified Monastrell.
labels: The grape, Mourvèdre in France and Mataro in Australia and California.
Own-rooted, ungrafted vines, a claim some old-vine Monastrells print.
The higher northern subzone of Yecla.
The historic black blending wine fermented on a double load of skins.

places.name: Jumilla
places.note: The Murcian town and municipality at the heart of the larger DO, surrounded by old ungrafted Monastrell on lime and sand at 400 to 700 metres; the premium bodegas of the 2000s revival cluster here.

places.name: Jumilla's Albacete portion
places.note: Six municipalities of Castilla-La Mancha, around Hellín, Tobarra and Ontur, higher and a little cooler, inside DO Jumilla despite the regional border; a trap because the wine is labelled Jumilla, not Castilla.

places.name: Yecla
places.note: The single-municipality DO north east of Jumilla, Monastrell on limestone with a pocket of international grapes, split into Campo Arriba, the high northern land of the best old vines, and Campo Abajo, the lower south.

places.name: Campo Arriba
places.note: Yecla's northern subzone, rising towards 800 metres, where old bush Monastrell on poor limestone gives the denomination's freshest and most structured wines.

places.name: Bullas
places.note: A third Murcian Monastrell DO, recognised in 1994, south west of Jumilla at higher altitude, small and little exported.

places.name: Alicante
places.note: The DO across the Valencian border to the east, Monastrell again, and home of Fondillón, a long-aged, unfortified, naturally strong sweet Monastrell matured in old casks.

places.name: Almansa
places.note: The Albacete DO to the north, on the road to Valencia, where Garnacha Tintorera, the red-fleshed Alicante Bouschet, makes inky reds beside Monastrell.

producers.name: Bodegas Juan Gil
producers.why: The Jumilla family house of the 2000s revival, whose Monastrell and the Cabernet-led El Nido blends made the region fashionable abroad.

producers.name: Casa Castillo
producers.why: A Jumilla estate working ungrafted old Monastrell on its own roots, the region's reference for site-driven, fresher wines.

producers.name: Bodegas Castaño
producers.why: Yecla's leading family house, whose Monastrell under the Hécula and Solanera labels defines the denomination for most drinkers.

producers.name: Bodegas Olivares
producers.why: A Jumilla house famous for Dulce Monastrell from old ungrafted bush vines, the reference for the sweet style.

producers.name: Bodegas Luzón
producers.why: A large Jumilla bodega making reliable young and oaked Monastrell at every price.

producers.name: Bodegas Barahonda
producers.why: A Yecla family house with old Monastrell in Campo Arriba and a modern range of blends.

producers.name: Bodegas Carchelo
producers.why: An early Jumilla modernist, blending Monastrell with Syrah and Cabernet in French oak from the 1990s.

producers.name: Bodegas San Isidro
producers.why: The Jumilla co-operative, among the largest in Spain, the source of much of the region's everyday Monastrell.

exam: Name the grape and its synonyms: Monastrell, Mourvèdre in France, Mataro in Australia and California.
Place both DOs in Murcia, inland and south east, and know that Jumilla crosses into Albacete while Yecla is one municipality.
Give the dates: Jumilla DO 1966, Yecla DO 1975, phylloxera in Jumilla 1989.
Describe the wine: dark, ripe, tannic, high in alcohol, from bush vines on limestone and sand, with Syrah and Cabernet as the modern partners.
Know Dulce Monastrell as the sweet red and Fondillón as Alicante's aged sweet Monastrell next door.
Say why the old vines are ungrafted: sandy soils kept phylloxera out until 1989.
traps: Monastrell is Mourvèdre; it is not Garnacha, not Mencía and not Bobal, which belongs to Utiel-Requena and Manchuela.
Monastrell is late ripening and needs heat; a candidate who calls it an early or cool-climate grape has it backwards.
Jumilla is one DO in two regions; wine from its Albacete villages is labelled Jumilla, not Castilla-La Mancha.
Yecla is a single municipality with two subzones, Campo Arriba and Campo Abajo; they are not two DOs.
Fondillón is Alicante's, not Jumilla's, and it is unfortified; Dulce Monastrell is Jumilla's sweet red.
Phylloxera reached Jumilla in 1989, a century after Rioja; the late date explains the ungrafted vines, not any immunity in the grape.

cards.f: The grape of Jumilla and Yecla, and its names abroad
cards.b: Monastrell: Mourvèdre in France (Bandol, the southern Rhône), Mataro in Australia and California. Late ripening, thick skinned, needs heat.

cards.f: How do DO Jumilla and DO Yecla differ in date and extent?
cards.b: Jumilla DO 1966, Murcia plus six municipalities of Albacete. Yecla DO 1975, a single municipality in Murcia with subzones Campo Arriba and Campo Abajo.

cards.f: Why Jumilla has so many ungrafted vines
cards.b: Sandy soils over limestone kept phylloxera away until 1989; old bush Monastrell on its own roots (pie franco) survives from before.

cards.f: Taste profile of Jumilla Monastrell
cards.b: Blackberry, dried fig, earth and game; high tannin and alcohol, soft when ripe; young unoaked or blended with Syrah and Cabernet in oak.

cards.f: Dulce Monastrell versus Fondillón
cards.b: Dulce Monastrell: Jumilla's sweet red, late harvest or fortified. Fondillón: Alicante's unfortified, naturally strong sweet Monastrell aged long in old casks.

cards.f: Jumilla and Yecla climate
cards.b: Continental with Mediterranean summers: over 3,000 sun hours, 40 °C afternoons, winter frost, about 300 mm of rain, 400 to 800 metres.

cards.f: Yecla's best subzone
cards.b: Campo Arriba, the higher northern land towards 800 metres, where old bush Monastrell on poor limestone gives the freshest, most structured wines.

questions.q: Which grape leads the red wines of both Jumilla and Yecla?
questions.exp: Monastrell, the Mourvèdre of France, is the grape of Murcia's hill country. Garnacha leads in Navarra and Priorat, Bobal in Manchuela and Utiel-Requena, Tempranillo in Rioja.

questions.q: What is Monastrell called in France?
questions.exp: Mourvèdre in Bandol and the southern Rhône, Mataro in Australia and California, Monastrell in Spain: one late-ripening, heat-loving grape.

questions.q: In which year did phylloxera finally reach Jumilla, a century after it devastated Rioja?
questions.exp: The sandy soils delayed the louse until 1989, which is why ungrafted old Monastrell survives. 1966 and 1975 are the DO dates of Jumilla and Yecla; 1901 is the era of Rioja's crisis.

questions.q: Which Spanish denomination consists of a single municipality in Murcia?
questions.exp: Yecla is the one-town DO, split into Campo Arriba and Campo Abajo. Jumilla crosses into Albacete, Bullas covers several Murcian towns, Almansa is in Albacete.

questions.q: Which subzone of Yecla, the higher northern land, is known for its old bush-vine Monastrell?
questions.exp: Campo Arriba rises towards 800 metres and holds the oldest vines on the poorest limestone; Campo Abajo is the lower, warmer south of the municipality.

questions.q: Into which neighbouring region does DO Jumilla extend from Murcia?
questions.exp: Six municipalities of Albacete, in Castilla-La Mancha, lie inside DO Jumilla. Valencia holds Alicante and Utiel-Requena; Andalucía and Aragón do not border the DO.

questions.q: What is the aged, unfortified sweet Monastrell of neighbouring Alicante called?
questions.exp: Fondillón is Alicante's naturally strong late-harvest Monastrell matured for years in old casks without fortification; Jumilla's sweet red is Dulce Monastrell.
