regions.name: Jerez (Sherry)
regions.summary: Sherry is the historic wine of the far south west, grown on blinding white albariza chalk around Jerez de la Frontera between the Guadalquivir and the Atlantic. Palomino dominates the dry styles; Pedro Ximénez and Moscatel make the sweet ones. Traditional fortification helps steer the ageing: at about fifteen per cent a yeast veil called flor grows and keeps Fino and Manzanilla pale and bone dry, at seventeen or more the flor dies and Oloroso ages in contact with air. Almost everything passes through a solera, a fractional blend of casks that has no vintage. Manzanilla is Fino aged in the sea air of Sanlúcar de Barrameda. Eligible dry wines can also reach their required strength without added spirit.

terroir.climate: Hot and maritime: around 300 days of sunshine, summers near 40 °C, mild wet winters and about 600 millimetres of rain, nearly all between autumn and spring. Two winds rule the year. The poniente blows damp and cool off the Atlantic and feeds the flor; the levante blows hot and dry from the east, stresses the vine, and is used to raisin grapes for sweet wine.
terroir.soils: Albariza, a soft white marl of chalk, clay and silica, so pale it hurts the eyes in summer. It soaks up the winter rain like a sponge, then bakes to a crust that seals the moisture in, so the vine drinks through the dry months. Barros, darker clay, and arenas, coastal sand, make up the rest; the finest Palomino and the Jerez Superior zone are albariza, and Moscatel grows on the sands near Chipiona.
terroir.topography: Gentle rolling hills, none above 150 metres, between the Guadalquivir marshes, the Atlantic beaches and the Bay of Cádiz, with the albariza crowning the slopes and the heavier soils in the hollows. The famous pagos, Macharnudo, Carrascal, Añina and Balbaína near Jerez and Miraflores near Sanlúcar, are the best of these low chalk hills.
terroir.water: The Guadalquivir meets the sea at Sanlúcar, and the river mouth's humidity and cooler air are why Manzanilla's flor lives all year. The Guadalete runs past Jerez to El Puerto de Santa María on the Bay of Cádiz. The Atlantic itself tempers the heat and supplies the poniente.

grapes.name: Palomino
grapes.styles: Palomino Fino, the principal grape for dry Sherry: neutral and low in acid as a table wine, which is exactly what flor and the solera need as a blank canvas.

grapes.name: Pedro Ximénez
grapes.styles: Sun-dried on mats until nearly a raisin, then fortified into the black, syrupy sweet Sherry called PX; much of it is grown in Montilla-Moriles and brought in as must under a long-standing permission.

grapes.name: Moscatel
grapes.styles: Moscatel de Alejandría from the sands around Chipiona, sun-dried for a grapey, orange-scented sweet Sherry lighter than PX.

grapes.name: Beba, Perruno and Vigiriega
grapes.styles: Historic pre-phylloxera varieties readmitted to the rulebook in 2023, then a curiosity in a few growers' hands.

wines.note: Typically Palomino aged entirely under flor, fourteen to seventeen per cent: pale, bone dry, almond, bread dough and brine. Serve cold from a fresh bottle with olives, jamón and fried fish, and finish the bottle within days.

Fino aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, where thicker year-round flor makes it lighter, saltier and sharper, with a camomile note; the classic glass with shellfish and the half-bottle an easy sell by the table.

A Fino whose flor has died or been removed, then aged in air, with refortification where needed: amber, dry, hazelnut and tobacco, sixteen to twenty-two per cent. Cool, not cold, with consommé, mushrooms, cured cheese or roast chicken.

Traditionally fortified to seventeen or more to suppress flor: mahogany, dry, walnut, leather and dried fruit with real weight. Serve at cellar temperature with game, oxtail, hard cheese or alone after dinner.
A wine that started as a Fino candidate and turned, carrying an Amontillado's nose on an Oloroso's body; rare, dry, and treated like Oloroso at the table.
Black, viscous, at least 212 grams of sugar: fig, raisin, coffee and liquorice. Pour small, slightly chilled, over vanilla ice cream or beside blue cheese.

Cream is Oloroso sweetened to 115 to 140 grams, raisined and soft; Pale Cream is a flor-aged wine sweetened with rectified must, pale and gentle, as the house pours it. Both take ice and a slice of orange, or a fruit tart.

made.viticulture: Palomino is trained low on the albariza, traditionally in the vara y pulgar system, a stick and a thumb, where one cane carries this year's crop and a spur prepares next year's, though trellised vineyards are common now. Spacing is wide and the vine is left to root deep into the chalk; the soil's crust and its water-holding marl are what carry the plant through a rainless summer at 40 °C. Harvest comes early, in late August and the first days of September, because Palomino needs only enough sugar for a base of about twelve per cent and must keep what little acidity it has. Grapes for PX and Moscatel are laid out on esparto mats in the sun for a week or more, a step called asoleo, until they are shrivelled and intensely sweet. The levante is the enemy during flowering and the friend during asoleo. Jerez Superior, the albariza heartland between Jerez, Sanlúcar and El Puerto, is where the best Palomino is grown; the classic pagos, Macharnudo, Carrascal, Añina and Balbaína, are low chalk hills to the north and west of the city.
made.winemaking: Palomino is pressed gently, the free-run juice kept for Fino, and fermented dry in stainless steel or, rarely, in butts. The young wine is classified with chalk marks on the cask: a palma for flor, a raya for a heavier wine bound for Oloroso. In traditional fortified production, fortification follows, with grape spirit blended half and half with wine: to about fifteen per cent for the flor candidates, so the yeast veil can grow across a butt filled five sixths full, and to seventeen or more for Oloroso, which kills the flor and lets the wine age in air. Flor feeds on alcohol and glycerol, makes acetaldehyde and shields the wine from oxygen; it needs humidity and mild warmth, so bodegas are high, airy and open to the poniente. Ageing runs through the criaderas and solera: wine is drawn from the solera, the oldest row, in the saca, and refilled from the next scale in the rocío, each topped up from the younger one, so every bottle blends many years at a legal average age of two years minimum. Biological ageing followed by oxidative ageing produces Amontillado, with refortification where needed; a palma that turns towards Oloroso weight is struck through as Palo Cortado. Sweetening comes last, with PX, Moscatel or rectified must, for Medium, Cream and Pale Cream. Seasoned oak butts are customary; the specification normally limits oak vessels to 1,000 litres. The current specification permits unfortified dry Jerez when its requirements are met. Biological and oxidative wines may use solera or static añada ageing.

law.classification: Three denominations share one Consejo: DO Jerez-Xérès-Sherry, DO Manzanilla-Sanlúcar de Barrameda and DO Vinagre de Jerez, Jerez from the 1933 statute that made it Spain's first regulated wine, Manzanilla a denomination of its own since 1964, the vinegar added later. The production zone covers ten municipalities of Cádiz and Seville: Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María, Sanlúcar de Barrameda, Chiclana, Chipiona, Puerto Real, Rota, Trebujena, Lebrija and San José del Valle. Ageing was for decades confined to the Sherry triangle of Jerez, El Puerto and Sanlúcar; the revised rulebook extends it to the production towns, with the one fixed rule that Manzanilla may only be aged in Sanlúcar. Styles are defined by biology and sugar: Fino, Amontillado, Oloroso and Palo Cortado are dry, normally no more than four grams a litre; Pale Cream, Medium and Cream are sweetened; PX and Moscatel are naturally sweet from raisined grapes. Age is certified by the Consejo for the oxidative styles at twelve and fifteen years, and as VOS at twenty and VORS at thirty, by analysis and tasting panel. The 2023 revision readmitted historic grapes, and the unfortified dry styles, approved in Brussels on 29 July 2025, came into force on 25 August 2025. The May 2026 specification permits a qualified-old-wine sugar exception tied to acidity; its analytical table and conditions should be read together. Fino ageing excludes Sanlúcar, the home of the separate Manzanilla denomination.

places.name: Jerez de la Frontera
places.note: The inland city that names the wine and holds the great bodegas, warmer and drier than the coast, where Fino is fuller and Oloroso and Amontillado reach their depth; Macharnudo, Carrascal, Añina and Balbaína are its classic albariza pagos.

places.name: Sanlúcar de Barrameda
places.note: The town at the mouth of the Guadalquivir where humidity and cooler sea air keep flor alive all year, so Manzanilla is lighter, sharper and saltier than Fino; Miraflores is its best pago, and Sanlúcar alone may age Manzanilla.

places.name: El Puerto de Santa María
places.note: The third town of the triangle, on the Bay of Cádiz, whose Finos sit between Jerez's weight and Sanlúcar's salt; a historic port for shipping the wine.

places.name: Macharnudo
places.note: The most famous pago, a high albariza hill north west of Jerez whose Palomino gives the most structured Finos and some of the greatest Amontillados.

places.name: Chipiona, Rota, Chiclana and Trebujena
places.note: Coastal and river towns of the wider production zone, Chipiona on sand for Moscatel, Trebujena on the Guadalquivir marsh edge, all allowed to age wine under the revised rules.

places.name: Montilla-Moriles
places.note: A separate DO inland in Córdoba, where Pedro Ximénez ripens so fully that its flor wines need no fortification and ferment in clay tinajas; much of Jerez's PX must comes from here, and its own Fino-style wines are a frequent exam comparison.

producers.name: González Byass
producers.why: The Jerez house founded in 1835 behind Tío Pepe, the world's reference Fino, and a great range of aged Amontillado and Palo Cortado.

producers.name: Emilio Lustau
producers.why: The house that brought almacenista Sherries, from small private stockholders, to the world and set the standard for Palo Cortado and East India Solera.

producers.name: Valdespino
producers.why: An old Jerez family house whose Inocente Fino, from the Macharnudo pago and fermented in butt, is the model single-vineyard Fino.

producers.name: Equipo Navazos
producers.why: A selectors' project bottling single casks from the great soleras of Jerez and Sanlúcar, the engine of the modern Sherry revival.

producers.name: Barbadillo
producers.why: The largest house of Sanlúcar, founded in 1821, whose Solear Manzanilla and sweetened Pale Cream are standards of the town.

producers.name: Hidalgo-La Gitana
producers.why: A Sanlúcar family house whose La Gitana Manzanilla is the style's most recognised bottle and whose Pasada shows what age does to flor.

producers.name: La Cigarrera
producers.why: A small Sanlúcar bodega dating from 1758 with a saline, fresh Manzanilla that pours well by the half-bottle.

producers.name: Osborne
producers.why: The El Puerto de Santa María house of 1772, known for the black bull on the hillsides and for its VORS Amontillado and Palo Cortado.

producers.name: Williams & Humbert
producers.why: A Jerez house founded in 1877 with Dry Sack and a run of certified single-vintage añada Sherries.

producers.name: Delgado Zuleta
producers.why: The oldest house of Sanlúcar, from 1744, with La Goya Manzanilla, a bar classic in Andalucía.

exam: Explain the traditional fortified pathway: fortify to about fifteen and flor lives for Fino and Manzanilla; fortify to seventeen or more and it dies for Oloroso; Amontillado has done both; Palo Cortado is the rarity between.
Name the grapes: Palomino for the dry styles, Pedro Ximénez and Moscatel for the sweet, and the soil, albariza.
Name the three towns of the triangle and say that Manzanilla is Fino aged in Sanlúcar, a place not a grape.
Explain a solera: fractional blending through criaderas, no vintage, average age two years minimum, VOS twenty and VORS thirty.

Give the standard May 2026 sugar bands in grams per litre: dry at most 4; Pale Dry 4 to below 50; Medium 4 to below 115; Pale Cream 50 to below 115; Cream 115 to 140; PX at least 212. Check the qualified-old-wine exception separately.
Serve it: Fino and Manzanilla cold and fresh, Amontillado cool, Oloroso and Palo Cortado at cellar temperature, PX slightly chilled.
Know the two winds, poniente and levante, and what each does to the flor and the harvest.
Know the recent changes: historic grapes in 2023, ageing allowed across the production zone, unfortified dry styles from August 2025.
traps: Manzanilla is Fino aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda; it is not a grape, not a sweet style, and the name has nothing to do with camomile tea beyond the aroma.
Fino and Oloroso differ in their ageing. The traditional fortification pathway helps explain flor management, but eligible dry Jerez need not be fortified.
Amontillado is dry; the sweetened version of an oxidative wine is Cream, and Pale Cream is a sweetened flor wine, not a light Cream.
Palo Cortado is a dry wine, not a halfway sweetness; it describes a cask that changed course.
A solera has no vintage; the only vintage Sherry is the rare añada, and VOS and VORS are average ages of twenty and thirty years, not minimum ages of each drop.
Pedro Ximénez is mostly grown in Montilla-Moriles, a separate DO in Córdoba, and only permitted into Jerez as must; do not call Montilla a Sherry.
Fino and Manzanilla are perishable once opened and served cold; Oloroso keeps for weeks and is served cool, not cold.

cards.f: The flor rule in one line
cards.b: Traditional pathway: fortify to about 15 per cent for flor ageing, or about 17 to suppress flor for Oloroso. Eligible dry Jerez can reach the required strength without added spirit; the ageing method defines the style.

cards.f: What is Manzanilla?
cards.b: Fino aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, where humid sea air keeps flor alive all year: lighter, saltier, sharper. A place, not a grape.

cards.f: How does Palo Cortado differ from Amontillado?
cards.b: Amontillado: a Fino whose flor died, then aged in air, with refortification where needed, dry. Palo Cortado: a flor candidate that turned, Amontillado nose on Oloroso body, dry.

cards.f: Sherry's main grapes and their jobs
cards.b: Palomino: the main dry-wine grape, not the only authorised variety. Pedro Ximénez: black sweet PX, sun-dried. Moscatel: lighter grapey sweet wine from the sands at Chipiona.

cards.f: Albariza: what it is and why it matters
cards.b: White chalky marl that soaks up winter rain and crusts in summer, feeding the vine through drought; the Jerez Superior zone and the great pagos are albariza.

cards.f: How a solera works
cards.b: Scales of old butts: wine is drawn (saca) from the solera, the oldest row, and refilled (rocío) from the criaderas above; a blend of many years with no vintage.

cards.f: Sherry sugar scale, grams per litre
cards.b: May 2026: dry at most 4; Medium 4 to below 115; Pale Cream 50 to below 115; Cream 115 to 140; Moscatel minimum 160; PX minimum 212. Qualified old wines have a conditional exception.

cards.f: VOS and VORS
cards.b: Certified average ages of 20 (Very Old Sherry) and 30 years (Very Old Rare Sherry), for Amontillado, Oloroso, Palo Cortado and PX only; 12 and 15 year marks sit below.

cards.f: The three towns of the Sherry triangle
cards.b: Jerez de la Frontera (inland, fuller wines), El Puerto de Santa María (bay, between), Sanlúcar de Barrameda (river mouth, Manzanilla only).

cards.f: Serving the styles
cards.b: Fino and Manzanilla: cold, fresh bottle, drink within days. Amontillado: cool. Oloroso and Palo Cortado: cellar temperature. PX: slightly chilled, small pour.

questions.q: Traditionally, which Sherry style is fortified to about seventeen per cent from the start of its ageing?
questions.exp: Oloroso is the traditional high-fortification answer. Eligible dry Jerez may now reach the required strength without added spirit; oxidative ageing distinguishes Oloroso, whereas Fino is biological and Amontillado combines the two.

questions.q: In which town must Manzanilla be aged?
questions.exp: Manzanilla is Fino aged at the mouth of the Guadalquivir in Sanlúcar, where the humid air keeps flor thick all year; the other three are production towns for Jerez.

questions.q: What is the name of the white chalky soil on which the best Palomino is grown?
questions.exp: Albariza is the pale marl of chalk, clay and silica that stores winter rain under a summer crust; barros and arenas are the clay and sand soils of lesser rank.

questions.q: Which grape is the principal variety for dry Sherry?
questions.exp: Palomino Fino, neutral and low in acid, is the principal canvas for flor and solera, rather than the only authorised dry-wine variety. Pedro Ximénez and Moscatel make the sweet wines; Airén is the plateau's brandy grape.

questions.q: What is the certified minimum average age of a VORS Sherry?
questions.exp: VORS, Very Old Rare Sherry, certifies thirty years of average age by analysis and tasting panel; VOS is twenty. Both apply only to Amontillado, Oloroso, Palo Cortado and PX.

questions.q: What is the living film of yeast that grows on the surface of a Fino cask called?
questions.exp: Flor consumes alcohol and glycerol, produces acetaldehyde and seals the wine from oxygen, which keeps Fino and Manzanilla pale, dry and saline.

questions.q: Which Sherry style began under flor and finished its ageing in contact with air?
questions.exp: Amontillado combines biological ageing followed by oxidative ageing, with refortification where needed: dry, amber and nutty. Fino is defined by biological ageing; Oloroso by oxidative ageing. An initial flor veil can precede Oloroso's oxidative stage. PX is a sweet raisined wine.

questions.q: What is the minimum residual sugar of a Pedro Ximénez Sherry in grams per litre?
questions.exp: PX requires at least 212 grams per litre. The May 2026 specification gives Cream 115 to 140, Pale Cream 50 to below 115 and Moscatel at least 160.
